corrected_value.title: Criticizing groups from the inside and the outside: An identity perspective on the intergroup sensitivity effect

decisions.location: Results: Classic ISE (Contrast 1) (also Results: Mediation analyses; Discussion; References)
decisions.quote: Parallel analyses of the self-report measures showed that Contrast 1 was significant for message motive, t(1,455) = -15.104, p < .001, r = .369, and for message threat, t(1,455) = 7.081, p < .001, r = .183. Consistent with the classic ISE (e.g., Hornsey & Imani, 2004) participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by outgroup criticism than ingroup criticism.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: In this pre-registered experiment (N = 1,459), the authors explicitly test the classic intergroup sensitivity effect (ISE; Contrast 1) on self-reported message motive and message threat ratings adapted from Hornsey and Imani (2004), reporting in Results (Section 4.2.1) that participants ascribed less constructive motives to and felt more threatened by outgroup criticism than ingroup criticism 'Consistent with the classic ISE (e.g., Hornsey & Imani, 2004)'. They further test and confirm in Section 4.4.3 ('Mediation analyses') and the Discussion the serial mediation process model (source -> message motive -> message threat -> behavior) attributed to Hornsey and Imani (2004) and Thürmer and McCrea (2018), reordering constructiveness before threat specifically to test this process. (2) Source-backed identity: Verified in the reference list and Crossref metadata as Hornsey, M. J., & Imani, A. (2004), 'Criticizing groups from the inside and the outside: An identity perspective on the intergroup sensitivity effect', Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 30(3), 365-383, DOI 10.1177/0146167203261295. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: The only shipped row (input_row_index 1731) is Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Motivation Science, 10.1037/mot0000097), a different paper by different authors; Hornsey and Imani (2004) is also distinct from all sibling candidates (Sutton et al., 2006, 2008; Thürmer et al., 2019).

corrected_value.authors: Sutton, R. M., Elder, T. J., & Douglas, K. M.
corrected_value.title: Reactions to internal and external criticism of outgroups: Social convention in the intergroup sensitivity effect

decisions.location: Results: Bystander ISE (Contrast 2) (also Introduction: Design; Discussion; References)
decisions.quote:
As predicted, a bystander ISE (Contrast 2) emerged for the selfreport measures of message motive, t(1,455) = -20.208, p < .001, r = .469, and message threat, t(1,455) = 13.341, p < .001, r = .331.
Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006), participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by between-group criticism than within-group criticism.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: The authors explicitly design their pure bystander ISE conditions (criticism of an uninvolved outgroup by a same-group vs. different-outgroup source) after Sutton et al. (2006) to provide a high-powered pre-registered replication and effect-size estimate of the bystander ISE (Contrast 2). In Results (Section 4.2.2), they report significant bystander ISE effects on self-reported message motive and message threat (as well as on behavioral bonus assignment), explicitly comparing their finding to Sutton et al. (2006). (2) Source-backed identity: Verified in the reference list and Crossref metadata as Sutton, R. M., Elder, T. J., & Douglas, K. M. (2006), 'Reactions to internal and external criticism of outgroups: Social convention in the intergroup sensitivity effect', Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 32(5), 563-575, DOI 10.1177/0146167205282992. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: Shipped row 1731 is Thürmer and McCrea (2018, 10.1037/mot0000097), which tested only the classic ingroup-target ISE and included no bystander conditions. Sutton et al. (2006) is also distinct from sibling target_index 3 (Sutton et al., 2008), as the source explicitly notes that Sutton et al. (2006) examined uninvolved bystanders alone without a direct comparison to classic ingroup-target ISE conditions, whereas Sutton et al. (2008) added that direct comparison.

corrected_value.authors: Sutton, R. M., Douglas, K. M., Elder, T. J., & Tarrant, M.
corrected_value.title: Social identity and social convention in responses to criticisms of groups

decisions.location: Introduction: Section 1.2 (also Contrasts and predictions; Results: Classic versus bystander ISE (Comparison I); Discussion; References)
decisions.quote:
Sutton et al. (2008) included such a comparison and found consistent evidence for both the classic ISE and the bystander ISE, with both effects being of similar magnitude.
Although their sample was sufficient to detect a medium-sized interaction, it did not provide sufficient power to detect a small effect. Given that interactions are typically smaller than main-effects, a high-powered test of this effect is warranted.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: In the Introduction (Section 1.2), the authors identify Sutton et al.'s (2008) finding that directly comparing classic ISE and bystander ISE conditions yielded consistent evidence for both effects with similar magnitude, and explicitly state that because Sutton et al. (2008) lacked statistical power to detect a small interaction difference, 'a high-powered test of this effect is warranted.' They operationalize this direct comparison as Comparison I (Contrast 1 minus Contrast 2) in Section 1.3.2, empirically test it in Results (Section 4.4.1, 'Classic versus bystander ISE (Comparison I)'), and contrast their finding (a significantly larger bystander ISE than classic ISE across measures) with the equal-magnitude pattern in the Discussion. (2) Source-backed identity: Verified in the reference list as the book chapter 'Sutton, R. M., Douglas, K. M., Elder, T. J., & Tarrant, M. (2008). Social identity and social convention in responses to criticisms of groups. In Y. Kashima, K. Fiedler, & P. Freytag (Eds.), Stereotype dynamics: Language-based approaches to the formation, maintenance, and transformation of stereotypes (pp. 339-365)', with no DOI printed in the source. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: Shipped row 1731 (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, 10.1037/mot0000097) did not include bystander ISE conditions, and sibling target_index 2 (Sutton et al., 2006, 10.1177/0146167205282992) did not include classic ISE conditions for direct comparison; thus Sutton et al. (2008) is a distinct original work reporting the direct comparison retested here.

corrected_value.authors: Thürmer, J. L., McCrea, S. M., & McIntyre, B. M.
corrected_value.title: Motivated collective defensiveness: Group members prioritize counterarguing outgroup criticism over getting their work done

decisions.location: Results: Identification (Section 4.4.2) (also Introduction; Experimental setup; Method: Materials and procedure; Discussion; References)
decisions.quote: We therefore examined whether the classic and bystander ISE effects were consistent across levels of identification. In line with previous research (Thürmer et al., 2019), Johnson-Neyman Analyses indicated that the behavioural classic ISE on participants' bonus payment decision was significant for those participants reporting medium-tohigh identification with their group (2.45 and above), but not for those reporting low identification (Figure 1a).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: In Experimental setup and Method, the authors explicitly state that they added a four-item ingroup identification measure adapted from Thürmer et al. (2019) that was not part of Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) in order to test whether the behavioral ISE is moderated by ingroup identification. In Results (Section 4.4.2, 'Identification') and the Discussion, they conduct Johnson-Neyman analyses and explicitly report replicating the finding of Thürmer et al. (2019) that the behavioral classic ISE is significant among participants with medium-to-high ingroup identification but not among low identifiers. (2) Source-backed identity: Verified in the reference list and Crossref metadata as Thürmer, J. L., McCrea, S. M., & McIntyre, B. M. (2019), 'Motivated collective defensiveness: Group members prioritize counterarguing outgroup criticism over getting their work done', Social Psychological and Personality Science, 10(3), 382-392, DOI 10.1177/1948550618762298. (3) Absence and non-equivalence: Shipped row 1731 is Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Motivation Science, 10.1037/mot0000097), which the source explicitly notes did not include the identification measure or test identification moderation in Experiment 3. Thürmer et al. (2019) is a separate study in a different journal examining counterarguing behavior and identification moderation, not an alternate report of shipped row 1731 or any sibling target.
